domains.name: ML Systems & Hardware
domains.summary: How the physical and architectural properties of accelerators, together with the software layers above them, determine what models can be trained and served at what cost. Every ML training or inference decision is a budget over FLOPs, bytes moved, and bytes resident, so a practitioner who cannot reason about the memory hierarchy cannot reason about feasibility. This domain covers the machine, the numeric formats that run on it, and the compilers and profilers that close the gap between a model graph and measured throughput.

subdomains.name: GPU Architecture, Performance Models and Compilers
subdomains.summary: The layered view of an AI workload: SIMT execution and memory hierarchy, roofline arithmetic-intensity analysis, CUDA/Triton kernel authoring, low-precision numeric formats, and ML compilers that fuse operators.

topics.name: GPU Architecture and the CUDA Programming Model
topics.definition: The design of NVIDIA GPUs as throughput-oriented SIMT machines (warps, streaming multiprocessors, a deep memory hierarchy, tensor cores, concurrent streams) and the CUDA model by which programmers expose parallelism to them.
topics.explanation: A GPU trades single-thread latency for aggregate throughput: hundreds of threads per SM execute in warps of 32 lanes under a single instruction stream (SIMT), so divergence within a warp serialises the divergent paths and memory-access coalescing determines whether global traffic arrives in one transaction or many. Latency is hidden rather than reduced: an SM keeps many warps resident and switches to a ready warp while others stall on memory, which is why occupancy (resident warps relative to the hardware maximum, limited by registers, shared memory and thread counts per block) is a first-order performance variable. High-bandwidth memory sits far from the compute units, so frameworks tile work into registers, then shared memory (the fast scratchpad each SM manages explicitly), then L2, then HBM; keeping a working set in the fast levels is the essence of kernel-level ML optimisation. Tensor cores are fixed-function matrix-multiply-accumulate units that execute a tile of mixed-precision MMA in one instruction, giving an order-of-magnitude speed-up over general-purpose FP32 pipes but only for shapes, layouts and precisions they support. CUDA expresses all of this through a grid of thread blocks that are independent and therefore schedulable in any order, plus streams and events for asynchronous copy/execute overlap, and the host API is mostly a mechanism for describing that decomposition. For ML engineers the practical consequences are everywhere: contiguous memory layouts and channel dimensions that align to 32 lanes, batch sizes that keep SMs busy, avoiding host-device synchronisation inside training loops, and knowing why a fused kernel beats three separate elementwise passes. Streams make data parallelism across GPUs and asynchronous prefetch of the next micro-batch possible.

topics.name: Roofline Analysis, Profiling and Performance Tuning
topics.definition: A method for bounding an operator's attainable performance by the lesser of machine peak FLOP/s and memory bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, plus the measurement discipline (profilers, counters, ablations) used to find which bound actually applies.
topics.explanation: The roofline model, introduced by Williams, Waterman and Shashikant, plots attainable performance against arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte of DRAM traffic). Below the machine balance point a kernel is bandwidth-bound and no clever math helps; above it, peak compute matters. For ML this is the single most useful back-of-the-envelope tool: a matmul of shape (M,K)x(K,N) has roughly 2MNK FLOPs and O(MK+KN+MN) bytes, so intensity grows with tile size, while attention on a sequence of length L naively moves L^2 elements, which is why IO-aware reimplementation gave such large gains. It also explains the asymmetry between LLM prefill (large, compute-bound GEMMs) and decode (one token at a time, so weights are read once per token and the workload is bandwidth-bound), and why batching tokens instead of requests changes throughput dramatically. Arithmetic intensity is a per-operation quantity but end-to-end time is a sum, so the practical workflow is: profile to get per-kernel time, bytes and FLOPs; compare against the roof; then apply the fix appropriate to the bound (fusion or larger tiles for bandwidth, better precision or tensor-core utilisation for compute, launch-count reduction for overhead-bound small ops). Profilers here are not optional: NVIDIA Nsight Compute/Systems, PyTorch's Kineto/profiler traces, and framework op-level timing give the same numbers, and ML practitioners should read a kernel timeline the way a software engineer reads a flame graph. A tuned ML system is usually one where the residual time has been pushed into a few large compute-bound kernels rather than hundreds of small ones. The model is a simplification, because it assumes DRAM is the only limit and ignores latency, synchronisation, and network cost, all of which matter in distributed training where the analogous bound is communication volume over link bandwidth.

topics.name: Numerical Formats and Mixed-Precision Training
topics.definition: The family of floating-point and integer formats used to store weights, activations and gradients, and the techniques (automatic mixed precision, loss scaling, stochastic rounding, scaling of accumulators) that let low-precision arithmetic train stably.
topics.explanation: Every format trades dynamic range (exponent bits) against mantissa precision. FP32 has about 7 decimal digits; TF32 keeps FP32 range with a 10-bit mantissa on tensor cores; BF16 keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent so the range is unchanged but only 7 mantissa bits are precise; FP16 halves storage but has a narrow range that overflows near 65504 and underflows in normal-number territory, which is exactly what happens to small gradients. FP8 comes in E4M3 (weights/activations) and E5M2 (gradients) variants, needing per-tensor or block scaling and careful casting rules. Integer formats (INT8, INT4) are fixed-point and require zero points and per-channel scales, so they compress more aggressively but are sensitive to outliers. In mixed-precision training, matmuls and activations run in the fast format while master weights and accumulators stay in FP32, and the optimizer states are updated from FP32 gradients or from loss-scaled low-precision gradients. Loss scaling multiplies the loss by a large power of two before the backward pass so that small gradient magnitudes survive FP16's underflow, then divides them before the update; its failure modes are well documented: overflow to inf/NaN from too large a scale (requiring dynamic rescaling and skipped updates), and silent divergence when the scale interacts with gradient clipping or with optimizers whose internal state is also low precision. Beyond overflow, the deeper hazards are accumulation error (summing many small contributions in low precision loses the small ones), catastrophic cancellation in softmax and layernorm, gradient sparsification through rounding to zero, and nondeterminism from atomics and reduction order. Modern stacks keep those numerics inside reductions: FlashAttention and tensor-core GEMMs accumulate in FP32 even with FP16/BF16 inputs, and layer norm/softmax typically run in FP32. Practitioners must be able to reason about error budget per format, why BF16 largely displaced FP16 for large training runs, why INT8/FP8 inference needs calibration data or block-wise scales, and why a loss-spike investigation includes checking whether the failure preceded a precision or clipping change.

topics.name: ML Compilers, Intermediate Representations and Operator Fusion
topics.definition: The software stack that turns a model description into efficient machine code: graph capture and rewriting, operator fusion, layout/tiling decisions, automatic kernel generation, and the intermediate representations (HLO/Triton/Tensor dialects) that make retargeting feasible.
topics.explanation: A framework executes an eager op-by-op program, which is flexible and easy to debug but loses the global view needed for optimisation: nothing knows that three consecutive elementwise ops can read their input once, or that a matmul's output layout can be chosen to suit the next kernel. Compilers recover that view. Tensor compilers such as XLA, TVM, TorchInductor and IREE capture a computation graph or trace, apply algebraic and layout rewrites, fuse operators into fewer kernels, select or generate tile sizes and memory plans, and emit PTX/C++/MLIR-driven code. Fusion has two flavours: horizontal (same op on different inputs, e.g. fused QKV projection) and vertical (chained ops collapsed so intermediates never reach DRAM), and vertical fusion is usually the win because it converts bandwidth-bound sequences into one pass. MLIR supplies the substrate: multiple dialects at different abstraction levels, from linalg/tensor operations down to loops and GPU primitives, letting projects share lowering passes instead of each writing a monolithic compiler. Triton takes a different route: instead of compiling a graph it exposes a tile-level Python-embedded DSL in which the programmer writes block-shaped math and the compiler handles thread mapping, shared memory and vectorisation, which is why hand-written kernels for attention and quantised GEMMs are now commonly Triton rather than CUDA. The trade-offs are real: compilation latency and cache invalidation, graph breaks when control flow escapes the captured region, dynamic shapes forcing specialised recompilation, and debugging a fused kernel that produces a subtly different number than the eager chain. Auto-tuning and search (TVM's schedule search, XLA's tile heuristics) shift cost from programmer time to compute time, and modern LLM serving stacks typically combine an eager trainer with a compiled or hand-kernel-optimised inference path.

topics.name: Accelerator Landscape and Hardware-Software Co-design
topics.definition: The range of AI accelerators beyond general-purpose GPUs (TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs, ASICs, and research architectures such as in-memory and neuromorphic chips), and the practice of co-designing model structures and hardware so each exploits the other's strengths.
topics.explanation: GPUs dominate because they are programmable and have a mature software stack, but their design carries the overhead of generality: caches, branch prediction, and a wide instruction set that an inner-loop matmul does not need. Domain-specific accelerators instead specialise the datapath. TPUs are systolic arrays: weight-stationary dataflows where each processing element multiplies and accumulates into a neighbour, eliminating much operand-fetch traffic and making dense matrix algebra cheap in exchange for rigidity about batch, shape and mesh topology, and requiring an XLA-style compiler to place work across a pod interconnect. NPUs in phones and laptops are small fixed-function engines sized for one or two popular workloads (attention blocks, convolutions, a limited quantisation set), and their performance depends more on whether the framework supports the operator than on headline TOPS numbers. FPGAs offer reconfigurable pipelines and predictable latency for unusual dataflows or inference at low batch, at the cost of long design cycles and limited arithmetic flexibility. In-memory and neuromorphic approaches attack the von Neumann bottleneck directly by doing accumulation in the memory array or by event-driven sparse spiking computation; they remain research-scale with real obstacles in precision, programming model and tooling. Co-design is where the leverage sits: model choices such as arithmetic per parameter, sparsity, quantisation tolerance, sequence parallelism, or Mixture-of-Experts routing shapes can be picked to suit a target machine, while hardware gains value only if compilers and operators exist for it. Evaluating an accelerator correctly requires normalising on the workload actually used (tokens/s at a batch size that fits, cost per inference, energy per token), not marketing TOPS, which typically quote sparse or unrealisable peak figures.

domains.name: Large-Scale Training Systems
domains.summary: Training a frontier model is a distributed-systems problem: parameters, gradients, activations and optimizer state exceed a single accelerator's memory, and the interconnect rather than the FLOPs often decides the wall-clock time. This subdomain covers how to split a model and a workload across thousands of devices, how to pay for the communication, how to hold activation memory down, and how to keep a months-long job correct, recoverable and reproducible.

subdomains.name: Parallelism and Communication
subdomains.summary: The orthogonal ways to split work across devices - data, tensor, pipeline, expert and sequence parallelism - and the collective operations and fabric that carry their traffic.

topics.name: Data Parallelism, ZeRO Stages and Fully Sharded Data Parallel
topics.definition: Replicating the model across workers and partitioning the batch, plus the family of techniques (ZeRO stages 1-3, FSDP, distributed optimizer, offloading) that shard optimizer state, gradients and parameters themselves instead of replicating them.
topics.explanation: Vanilla synchronous data parallelism replicates the full model on every rank and all-reduces gradients, so throughput scales with rank count but memory per device does not shrink: weights, gradients and (crucially) optimizer state, which for Adam is two FP32 buffers plus an FP32 master copy, dominate the footprint - roughly 16 bytes per parameter in FP32 Adam plus activations. Gradient accumulation amortises communication over several micro-batches, and bucketing overlaps all-reduce with the backward pass, which is where DDP gets most of its scalability. ZeRO observes that all this replicated state is redundant and removes it stage by stage: stage 1 shards optimizer state, stage 2 adds gradient shards via reduce-scatter, stage 3 additionally shards parameters, gathering each layer's parameters just-in-time with all-gather and freeing them after use. That converts memory savings into extra communication, so stage 3 wants a fast intra-node fabric and careful prefetching; FSDP is the PyTorch-native realisation of stage-3-style sharding with a per-unit sharding strategy and mixed precision attached. Activation memory remains untouched by ZeRO, which is why it is combined with recomputation, and the whole budget is typically written per parameter as weights + gradients + optimizer + activations, then compared to HBM capacity. Combined with mixed precision, sharding raises subtleties: all-gather must move the low-precision copy while reduce-scatter may be in gradient precision, and the master weights live only on the owning rank, so checkpoint formats must be sharded-aware. The practical decision rule is that data parallelism is the cheapest scaling axis (perfect compute efficiency, traffic proportional to gradient size), so one exhausts DP/ZeRO before reaching for model parallelism.

topics.name: Tensor Parallelism and Sequence/Context Parallelism
topics.definition: Splitting individual tensor operations across devices (intra-layer/model parallelism) and splitting the sequence dimension so activations are distributed, as in Megatron-style column/row parallelism, tensor-sequence parallelism, Ulysses and ring attention.
topics.explanation: When one layer's weights or activations do not fit on a device, the arithmetic itself is partitioned. Megatron-LM splits an MLP's two matmuls so the first is column-parallel (each rank holds a slice of the output features, so the input needs no communication) and the second row-parallel (partial sums are all-reduced), and splits attention by heads so each rank computes a subset of heads; per transformer layer this costs a small constant number of all-reduces in the forward and backward passes. Because that traffic is per layer and per step, tensor parallelism is confined to a high-bandwidth domain - typically inside a node across NVLink - and kept to a modest degree (2-8) with data parallelism wrapped around it. It also shards activations, unlike data parallelism, so it is the standard answer for very wide models. The residual activation memory and the replicated layernorm/dropout path motivated Megatron's tensor-sequence parallelism: the sequence dimension is scattered so that non-tensor-parallel regions (layernorm, dropout, loss) operate on a per-rank sequence slice with all-gather/reduce-scatter instead of all-reduce, restoring memory savings while keeping the same communication volume. For long contexts, pure activation sharding is not enough, since attention's quadratic intermediates dominate; approaches include ring attention (pass K/V blocks around a device ring so each rank computes partial attention with online-softmax rescaling), DeepSpeed/Ulysses-style all-to-all head redistribution (each rank owns all heads for a sequence slice, converting sequence parallelism into head parallelism), and combinations with paged attention kernels. The engineering discipline is the same in every variant: enumerate the collectives per layer, their sizes, and whether the fabric supports them, then check that compute-to-communication did not collapse. Combined 4D layouts (data x tensor x pipeline x expert) make these choices interacting, which is where parallelism search frameworks such as Alpa and auto-placement tools enter.

topics.name: Pipeline Parallelism and Microbatch Schedules
topics.definition: Partitioning a model's layers into stages mapped to different devices and streaming micro-batches through them, with a schedule determining when each stage runs forward and backward passes and how much of the pipeline is idle.
topics.explanation: Pipeline parallelism is the cheap way to add depth to a cluster: communication is only activation tensors flowing between adjacent stages, so it tolerates slower inter-node links, which is why very large runs combine small tensor-parallel groups with wide pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas. The cost is the bubble. In GPipe's original schedule, all micro-batch forward passes run, then all backward passes in reverse; the idle fraction is roughly (p-1)/(m+p-1) for p stages and m micro-batches, so you need m several times p to be efficient, and memory grows with the number of in-flight activations. 1F1B interleaves one forward with one backward, holding peak in-flight micro-batches bounded and reducing activation memory at the cost of a modestly larger bubble; interleaved/v-pipeline schedules (Megatron) let a device own non-contiguous layer blocks to shrink the bubble further at the price of more memory and traffic. Zero-bubble and related schedules attack the residual idleness by splitting the backward pass into gradient-with-respect-to-input and gradient-with-respect-to-weight phases and placing them into bubble slots, or by using microbatch-distillation-style approximations; these show real gains only when the schedule overhead does not erase them. Schedules also interact with reliability: pipeline stage failure stalls the whole job, and stage imbalance from uneven layer counts creates persistent stalls. Finally, pipeline parallelism couples awkwardly with loss and optimizer placement, with activation checkpointing (recompute may be cheaper than holding cross-stage activations), and with expert layers, which want a different parallel axis. The right competency is to draw a schedule as a time-space diagram, compute bubble and peak memory for it, and pick the schedule for the model's depth and the cluster's link speeds.

topics.name: Mixture-of-Experts and Expert Parallelism
topics.definition: Sparsely activated transformer layers in which a learned router sends each token to a few expert FFNs, and the parallelism strategy that distributes experts across devices with all-to-all token exchange.
topics.explanation: An MoE layer replaces one dense FFN with N experts and a gating network that picks top-k per token, so total parameters grow while FLOPs per token stay near dense-equivalent; this decouples capacity from compute cost and is the reason trillion-parameter-class models can be trained and served economically. The systems burden is routing. Tokens must be dispatched to whichever device holds their chosen expert and results returned, which is an all-to-all collective whose volume depends on sequence length, hidden size and k, and all-to-all is the least friendly traffic pattern for hierarchical fabrics - it crosses nodes, cannot be overlapped as easily as all-reduce, and is sensitive to load imbalance. Load balancing is therefore a first-class concern: routers exhibit rich-get-richer behaviour, so auxiliary load-balancing losses, expert dropout, capacity factors with token dropping, or bias-based no-aux-loss balancing (Switch, GShard, StoMEx-style) are used, and capacity-factor choices trade dropped tokens against wasted compute. Sharded MoE replicates experts across ranks so that all-to-all can be replaced by all-reduce at the cost of memory; expert-parallel MoE moves experts to their own device group, usually nested with tensor and data parallelism so that an EP group sits inside the DP group. Training stability adds subtleties: router logits need precision care, the auxiliary loss perturbs optimisation and scaling, and checkpointing must handle routed-state and non-deterministic token assignment for reproducibility. At inference, MoE makes memory-bandwidth accounting unusual, because only the activated experts' weights are read per token but batch composition changes which experts are hot, which interacts with expert offloading and with paged KV-cache scheduling. Sparsity also breaks dense-kernel assumptions: grouped/batched GEMM kernels and token permutation cost real time.

topics.name: Collective Communication and Interconnect Fabrics
topics.definition: The collective operations (all-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather, all-to-all, broadcast, barrier) that distributed training depends on, their algorithms, and the physical fabrics (NVLink, PCIe, InfiniBand, Ethernet with RDMA) that determine their cost.
topics.explanation: Synchronous data parallelism reduces to one primitive: every rank must obtain the sum of gradients. Naively that is a gather to rank 0 plus a broadcast, whose traffic concentrates on one node; ring all-reduce instead arranges ranks in a ring and performs reduce-scatter followed by all-gather, so each rank sends and receives about 2(n-1)/n times the gradient size regardless of n, which is bandwidth-optimal and is why it became the standard. Tree and double-binary-tree algorithms trade latency for bandwidth and win at large rank counts or when message sizes are small, and modern libraries such as NCCL choose algorithms per message size and topology. Reduce-scatter and all-gather are the constituent halves: ZeRO-2 leans on reduce-scatter, ZeRO-3/FSDP add all-gather of parameters each step, and MoE dispatch needs all-to-all, whose cost is dominated by the slowest link in the crossing pattern. On the hardware side, PCIe is host-attached and comparatively narrow; NVLink/NVSwitch give intra-node GPU-to-GPU bandwidth an order of magnitude higher; RDMA-capable fabrics (InfiniBand, RoCE/Ethernet) let GPUs read remote memory directly, bypassing the CPU, and GPUDirect RDMA extends that to NIC-to-GPU. Rail-optimised and multi-rail node designs, fat-tree/dragonfly-ish topologies, and congestion control determine whether the theoretical bisection is achieved. Performance is usually reported as bus bandwidth, but the real skill is algorithm design: overlap communication with computation by partitioning into buckets on separate streams, choose collective granularity, avoid global barriers where a dependency ordering suffices, and keep the traffic pattern inside the fast fabric whenever the parallelism axis allows. Network failures, slow links, and straggler ranks are also communication phenomena, and they show up as unexplained throughput loss long before any compute problem exists.

topics.name: Activation Memory: Checkpointing, Recomputation and Offloading
topics.definition: Techniques that reduce the dominant part of training memory - saved forward activations needed by backpropagation - through selective or full recomputation, CPU/NVMe offload, layout choices, and operator-level fusion.
topics.explanation: Backpropagation needs the forward intermediates of each layer, so activation memory grows with layers, batch size, sequence length and hidden width, and for long-context transformers it exceeds parameter and optimizer memory by a large margin. Activation checkpointing stores only the outputs of coarse boundaries and recomputes the discarded intermediates during the backward pass, converting one extra forward pass into roughly a third more total compute and turning activation memory from linear in depth into sublinear. That trade is only sometimes worth it: recomputation costs real FLOPs, so the standard menu is full, selective (recompute only the cheap-but-large things like attention softmax statistics), per-layer granularity, and the Megatron-style combination of tensor-sequence parallelism plus selective recompute that recovers most of the memory without paying a full extra forward. Offloading moves activations, weights, or optimizer state to CPU RAM and even NVMe (ZeRO-Offload/Infinity), which increases capacity at the price of PCIe bandwidth and synchronisation - and offload is often better justified as a way to buy batch size than as a throughput win. Layout and fusion matter more than people expect: contiguous tensor layouts, avoiding duplicated copies in residual paths, in-place ops where autograd permits, and IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention that never materialise the L x L matrix, which is the single biggest long-context memory saving available. Gradient accumulation reduces the number of synchronisation-required samples rather than memory, but enables larger effective batch at fixed activation cost per micro-batch. The competent practitioner builds a memory budget table (weights, gradients, optimizer, activations, workspace/allocator fragmentation, communication buffers), measures peak rather than estimating from theory, and understands that allocator fragmentation and caching pools can make a job OOM at a memory level below the theoretical limit.

subdomains.name: Long-Run Reliability, Checkpointing and Cluster Scheduling
subdomains.summary: Multi-week jobs on thousands of accelerators fail routinely; the systems question is how to keep goodput high through checkpointing strategy, failure detection and recovery, deterministic restarts, and schedulers that allocate whole jobs efficiently.

topics.name: Long-Run Training Reliability, Checkpointing and Cluster Scheduling
topics.definition: The engineering that keeps a multi-week, thousands-of-accelerators job making progress: fault detection and recovery, checkpoint frequency and format, restart determinism, training-forensics of loss spikes, and cluster scheduling that maximises useful throughput.
topics.explanation: At frontier scale, hardware failure is not an exception but the operating condition. With a per-device mean-time-to-failure of weeks, a 2000-GPU job experiences interruptions every few hours, so the run must be planned around them: state saved frequently, recovery automated, and lost steps bounded. Checkpointing strategy is an economic calculation - checkpoint interval trades lost work against time spent writing (and the storage bandwidth it consumes), so asynchronous, sharded and incremental checkpoint formats, in-memory staging, and network-attached checkpointing exist precisely to make writes cheap enough to checkpoint often. A checkpoint must carry not only parameters and optimizer state but RNG state, data-loader position, scheduler state and the exact iteration boundary, otherwise restarting produces a job that is statistically different from the one that would have continued; reproducibility demands the same determinism controls (fixed kernel reduction order, seeded data shuffling, logged config and code revision). Loss spikes are a different failure class: data ordering, a bad batch, precision changes, optimizer hyperparameters, or a transient hardware fault can all cause them, and forensics means reconstructing per-rank step statistics, gradient norms, per-layer activation statistics, loss contributions per data shard, and comparing against a deterministic rerun of the affected window. Llama-3-class reports describe detecting, quarantining and mitigating spikes with data-order and hyperparameter changes over a months-long run, and this is a normal part of large runs rather than an anomaly. Cluster scheduling then determines whether the machine is used: gang scheduling with backfill, topology-aware placement to keep jobs on the fewest rails, pre-emption policies, priority and fair-share, and utilisation accounting (jobs held for a maintenance window, straggler nodes, or an over-subscribed interconnect waste real money). Goodput - useful training throughput after failure and recovery cost - is the metric that ties all of it together, and the honest framing is that reliability engineering is a compute-efficiency discipline, not a nicety. ML jobs are not like web services: they request hundreds or thousands of devices that must start together, hold specific network adjacency, and cannot be served from a partial allocation. That breaks ordinary schedulers. Gang scheduling and all-or-nothing placement guarantee that a job runs only when its full allocation exists, which prevents deadlock but invites fragmentation; backfill and priority tiers let small jobs slip between large reservations while protecting the frontier job's progress. Topology matters economically because two jobs placed on the same rails and switches can saturate a shared uplink, so good schedulers and good ML engineers reason about rack/rail locality, not just device counts. Pre-emption and spot-style allocation reduce cost when checkpointing and recovery are trustworthy, and their viability is entirely a function of how expensive restart is - which links scheduling back to the checkpoint topic. Utilisation must be reported as goodput: fraction of allocated device-hours actually making forward progress, excluding time lost to failures, restarts, data loading starvation, and comm-bound underutilisation; a cluster at 100% allocation can be at 55% goodput and the remedy differs completely depending on which loss dominates. Related practical concerns are storage and data-loading as schedulable resources (a job starved by a cold dataset is a scheduling failure), multi-tenancy fairness across research versus production queues, and the feedback loop in which cost per run determines which parallelism layout is chosen. Measurement infrastructure - per-job telemetry, per-node health metrics, and cost attribution to projects - is part of the systems work, not an afterthought.

domains.name: Inference Systems
domains.summary: Serving a trained model is a distinct engineering discipline: autoregressive decoding has a per-token sequential dependency, its cost is dominated by moving weights and KV cache rather than by arithmetic, and user-facing latency targets collide with the batching that makes hardware economical. This domain covers serving architecture and scheduling, memory management, decoding acceleration, compression and portability, and the retrieval indexes that surround modern LLM applications.

topics.name: Continuous Batching, SLOs and Serving Economics
topics.definition: Serving an LLM by admitting and retiring requests at the granularity of a single decode iteration (iteration-level or continuous batching), together with the latency/service objectives and cost model that determine how a serving fleet should be configured.
topics.explanation: Static batching, where a fixed set of requests runs to a fixed length, wastes most of the machine because generated lengths vary wildly: slots stay reserved after a request has finished, and the batch cannot change until the whole group ends. Orca introduced iteration-level scheduling: the engine runs one decode step at a time and rebuilds the batch after every step, so finished requests release their slots immediately and new requests join mid-flight, with selective batching applying the same attention computation to differently-sized per-request state. Effective batch size is what makes bandwidth-bound decode economical - throughput scales almost linearly with tokens per step while per-token weight traffic stays fixed - so continuous batching routinely yields several-fold capacity gains at the same latency. Latency must be decomposed to be managed: time to first token is governed by prefill work and queueing, time between tokens by decode step time plus scheduling delay, and end-to-end by total generated tokens; an SLO is usually a joint constraint (TTFT and TPOT percentiles), and the right objective is goodput, the throughput of requests that actually satisfy the SLO rather than raw tokens per second. Queueing intuition applies directly: as utilisation approaches one, waiting time explodes, so fleets are provisioned with headroom and autoscaled on queue depth rather than on average utilisation, and priority classes (interactive versus batch) let low-prefill work be deferred. Chunked prefill and decode co-scheduling, described in the disaggregation topic, is the main tool for keeping a decode-heavy batch fed without violating TTFT. Serving many fine-tuned variants multiplies the problem, which is why multi-LoRA engines batch a base model with many adapters rather than replicating servers per adapter. Finally, economics: cost per million tokens is (device hourly cost x number of devices) divided by accepted tokens per hour, and energy per token follows the same shape, so the decisions above are all cost decisions; reporting throughput without the accompanying latency percentiles and batch configuration is not a defensible benchmark.

topics.name: KV Cache Management and PagedAttention
topics.definition: Management of the key/value tensors cached during autoregressive decoding, whose size grows with batch and context length, and the paging abstraction that stores them in fixed-size blocks with an indirection table to eliminate fragmentation.
topics.explanation: Autoregressive decoding reuses every previous token's key and value vectors, so the cache is not an optional memoisation but exact computation state whose footprint is roughly 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x sequence_length x bytes x requests. That quantity grows linearly in both batch and context, is reserved per request, and quickly exceeds the memory needed for the weights, which is what caps concurrent requests. Conventional engines allocate a contiguous buffer per request sized by a maximum length, so most reserved memory is unusable padding and external fragmentation limits the batch; PagedAttention (vLLM, SOSP 2023) instead stores KV in fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens) and gives each request a block table mapping logical position to physical block, exactly like virtual memory. That makes allocation grow with actual generated length, enables sharing of blocks between sequences - most valuably for common prompt prefixes, where reference counting plus copy-on-write allows one cached prefill to serve many requests - and lets the scheduler decide admission based on blocks available rather than worst-case length. Prefix caching generalises this to a radix/tree-structured cache across requests, which is the main reason applications with long shared system prompts, multi-turn conversations or agent loops see first-token latency and cost drop dramatically. The cost of paging is indirection: attention kernels must gather non-contiguous blocks, so block size, layout and kernel design matter, and the paged form is what makes many attention kernels engine-specific. Cache pressure is relieved by several orthogonal levers: quantising KV to fp8 or int4, sliding-window and local-global attention patterns with sink tokens, eviction or summarisation of old context, and offload of cold blocks to CPU DRAM or SSD, which becomes the central resource in disaggregated and cache-centric serving architectures. The engineering competency is arithmetic: predict KV bytes for a given model and context, compare to available HBM, and know which lever (paging, quantisation, eviction, offload, or more replicas) buys what.

topics.name: Prefill/Decode Disaggregation and Phase-Aware Scheduling
topics.definition: Running the prompt-processing (prefill) phase and the token-generation (decode) phase on separate pools of accelerators, with independent parallelism, placement and scheduling for each, rather than interleaving both phases in one engine.
topics.explanation: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one large, essentially compute-bound pass and produces the initial KV cache; decode then emits tokens one at a time, reading weights and growing KV, and is bandwidth-bound. Colocating them creates mutual interference: a long prefill blocks the decode steps of everyone sharing that replica, so inter-token latency spikes for already-started requests, and the two phases want different batch sizes, precisions, tensor-parallel degrees and even different hardware. Disaggregation - separating prefill and decode pools, transferring the KV cache between them - lets each pool be optimised for its own roofline and its own SLO term, and DistServe framed the objective precisely as goodput maximisation under TTFT and TPOT constraints, showing substantial capacity gains over colocated scheduling. Production systems such as Mooncake push the design further into a KV-cache-centric architecture that pools CPU DRAM, SSD and RDMA fabric as a shared cache tier, using cross-request reuse plus cache-aware scheduling to raise effective capacity. The costs are real and worth knowing: KV transfer volume grows with prompt length, layers and precision, so a slow or congested fabric turns migration into the bottleneck; the scheduler must place prefill so that its output lands where decode capacity and prefix reuse agree; and the two pools must be sized and autoscaled jointly, which is harder than scaling one homogeneous pool. The alternative to disaggregation keeps phases colocated but makes them mixable: chunked prefill splits a long prompt into blocks and interleaves them with decode steps in the same batch, which recovers much of the tail-latency problem with none of the migration cost - the honest framing is that chunked prefill is a scheduling fix while disaggregation is a placement fix, and both address the same asymmetry. Multi-adapter serving, request migration for preemption, and speculative decoding all interact with these choices, so a serving stack should be evaluated as a system rather than a pile of optimisations.

topics.name: Speculative Decoding and Decoding-Time Acceleration
topics.definition: Generating several candidate tokens cheaply with a draft mechanism and verifying them in one pass of the target model, accepting the longest prefix that passes and thereby converting sequential decode steps into parallel verification.
topics.explanation: Decode latency is bound by the sequential dependency between tokens and by weight reads rather than arithmetic, which means a target model can score several candidate tokens in the time it takes to produce one - the free capacity that speculative decoding exploits. A draft source proposes gamma tokens; the target model evaluates them in a single forward pass; the standard algorithm (Leviathan et al.; independently Chen et al.) accepts each token while the target agrees, and on the first disagreement samples from the renormalised residual distribution, which provably leaves the output distribution exactly equal to the target model's - an important point, since the goal is faster sampling, not a cheaper approximation of it. Expected speed-up is governed by the acceptance rate alpha and draft cost: with per-token acceptance probability alpha, the expected accepted length is (1 - alpha^(gamma+1))/(1 - alpha), so a cheap but poorly aligned drafter or a gamma chosen too large both fail to help, and a drafter that is expensive relative to the target can make things worse. Draft sources include a smaller model from the same family, self-drafting heads trained on the target (Medusa's multiple decoding heads; EAGLE's feature-level autoregressive drafting), static n-gram or prompt-lookup drafting that costs nothing at inference time, and multi-token prediction objectives trained into the model itself; tree or multi-candidate verification lets one pass check several draft continuations at once. The interaction with batching is the crucial operational subtlety: at high batch, verification is no longer free because the machine is already compute-saturated and the extra tokens consume real FLOPs, so speculative decoding typically improves single-stream latency and hurts aggregate throughput unless the acceptance rate is high and the batch modest. Adjacent latency tricks share the same analysis: CUDA graphs and kernel fusion to remove launch overhead at decode, FlashDecoding-style parallelisation over KV length, early exit or layer skipping (approximate, not exact), and quantisation of weights to reduce bytes read per step.

topics.name: Quantisation, Pruning and Distillation for Deployment
topics.definition: Reducing the memory, bandwidth and compute a deployed model requires - through weight/activation quantisation, sparsity and pruning, or knowledge distillation into a smaller student - and measuring the quality that is lost per unit of saving.
topics.explanation: Deployment compression starts from an accounting of what limits the target: decode-time cost is dominated by bytes of weight and KV cache read per token, so weight-only quantisation to int8 or int4 is usually the highest-leverage change, whereas compute-bound prefill and training benefit more from structure and kernel choices. Post-training quantisation methods differ in how they choose scales and absorb error. Round-to-nearest with per-channel scales is the baseline; GPTQ performs layer-wise compensation using approximate second-order (Hessian) information from calibration data; AWQ observes that a small fraction of channels are salient because of large activation magnitudes and protects them by scaling; SmoothQuant migrates activation outlier difficulty into the weights so that int8 activations become feasible; block-wise and microscaling formats trade a small metadata overhead for much better tolerance of heavy-tailed distributions. Activation quantisation is harder than weight quantisation precisely because of impulse channels and because scales must be calibrated without hurting the model, while KV-cache quantisation is now routine at fp8. Pruning removes parameters: unstructured magnitude or second-order methods (SparseGPT, Wanda) can zero most weights with modest quality loss but rarely yield large-batch speed-up, whereas semi-structured 2:4 patterns have hardware support on some accelerators, and structured pruning of heads, layers or experts actually reduces FLOPs but usually requires retraining or distillation to recover quality. Distillation trains a student against a teacher's outputs: soft-target logit distillation is the classical form, and for LLMs the practical recipe is generation-based distillation, where teacher outputs become training data (this is how many open and on-device models are produced) - the honest caveat being that the student inherits the teacher's failure modes and style. Distillation is also the cheapest path to a smaller model when no teacher logits are available, and it interacts with everything: quantisation-aware training, calibration after compression, and re-validation of slice-level and safety behaviour. Measurement discipline decides everything: report task accuracy, calibration (ECE/Brier), and latency/memory at realistic batch, not perplexity alone.

topics.name: Model Packaging, Portability and Edge Deployment
topics.definition: Serialising a trained model so that a different runtime or device can execute it - exchange graphs, weight containers, runtimes and delegates - and the memory, thermal and security constraints that decide whether that model can run at the edge.
topics.explanation: A checkpoint produced by one framework version is not automatically a portable artifact. Graph exchange formats such as ONNX describe the computation as a model with a versioned operator set, tensor initialisers and dynamic-shape annotations; a runtime (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO, Core ML, NNAPI delegates) then applies layout optimisations, fuses operators, selects kernels and may quantise the graph. Portability in practice is a coverage problem: a model is portable to the extent that every operator exists on the target at the shape and precision required, and unsupported ops cause silent fallbacks to slower paths, which is why the correct evaluation is a measured end-to-end run on device rather than an export success. LLM-era containers differ from classical graph export because decoding is a loop with growing state: formats such as GGUF bundle quantised weights plus metadata for llama.cpp-style runtimes, while ExecuTorch and TFLite target mobile with explicit memory planning, delegate dispatch to NPUs/GPUs, and a pre-packaged program rather than a live graph. The security story matters and is often ignored: Python pickle-based checkpoints execute arbitrary code on load, so untrusted model files are a real supply-chain attack surface; PyTorch's weights_only loading path and container formats that carry only data (safetensors, memory-mapped tensor files) exist to remove that execution step, and organisations should still verify artifact provenance and signature rather than trusting a filename. Edge deployment is bounded by more than FLOPs: the sum of weights, KV cache and runtime buffers must fit in the device's usable RAM, sustained throughput is limited by thermal throttling and battery policy, and update distribution is a fleet-operations problem. The right mental model is a joint budget - bytes, peak memory, energy per inference, and time-to-first-token on a cold load - and an honest benchmark methodology, which is what suites like MLPerf (including its mobile and client benchmarks) try to standardise.

topics.name: Vector Search and Approximate Nearest Neighbour Indexes
topics.definition: Indexes that answer approximate k-nearest-neighbour queries over high-dimensional embeddings - graph, inverted-file and quantised structures - traded against recall, latency, memory and build cost, including filtering and freshness requirements.
topics.explanation: Exact search over N vectors of dimension d costs O(Nd) per query, which is unaffordable once N reaches millions or a query budget is a few milliseconds, so retrieval systems answer approximately: they accept a small probability of missing a true neighbour in exchange for orders-of-magnitude less work, and quantify the trade-off with recall@k measured against exact ground truth. Graph indexes such as HNSW build a multi-layer navigable small-world graph, greedily descending from sparse long-range layers to a dense base layer; efSearch and M tune the exploration/latency curve, and the structure handles incremental inserts well while deletions and tombstones degrade it. Inverted-file indexes cluster vectors into Voronoi cells with a coarse quantiser and scan only the nprobe closest cells; pairing IVF with product quantisation compresses each vector into codes from several small dictionaries so many candidates can be scored from RAM-resident codes (with optional re-ranking using the stored original vectors), which is how billion-scale search fits in a server. ScaNN's anisotropic quantisation is the sharpest theoretical idea in this area: quantisation error should be penalised along the direction of the query rather than isotropically, because only the inner-product component along the query changes ranking - so the loss function that decides code assignment is asymmetric. Disk-oriented graph designs (DiskANN-style) keep the index on SSD with compressed in-memory navigation, GPU implementations exploit massive parallel distance evaluation, and filtered search - where metadata predicates must be honoured - is genuinely harder than post-filtering, since an index traversal can wander into regions that all fail the predicate; practical designs combine attribute filtering with either pre-filtered candidate sets or predicate-aware graph traversal. Evaluation must report recall@k, queries per second, p99 latency, memory per vector, and build/update time under a realistic query and filter distribution, because a configuration that wins on one axis usually loses on another; downstream relevance evaluation (nDCG, hit rate of a retrieval-augmented pipeline) is a separate question from ANN quality, and the embedding model's quality dominates it.
